articles.title: Holly Throsby: ‘I was proud to not make a breakup album’
articles.summary: The writer and musician on returning to music, finding herself, and why right now is a terrifying time to be an artist. Holly Throsby does not enjoy having her photo taken. There’s even a song on her new album about it.
body: Walking along various bush tracks is a daily ritual for Throsby. A sense of nature gently pervades her seventh album, Normal Magic. It is in the imagery of sparkling water and swims; gardens and birds; bushfires and wind and rain on the roof. The album itself feels like the breaking of a drought: her first solo record in nine years. In the intervening time, she moved to the New South Wales south coast, had her second child, wrote her third novel, and recorded and toured a second album with Seeker Lover Keeper, her collaborative project with Sarah Blasko and Sally Seltmann. She has hardly been idle.

And yet, at 47, she says “there are a lot of things, particularly if you have children, that take you away from the work. I sometimes forget that I’m an artist altogether – for long periods, years. I forget that I’m a musician.”

It’s a startling statement from someone who picked up a guitar at the age of eight. “When I was a teenager, I would get home from school and write songs all afternoon, every afternoon, obsessively,” she says. “It’s been nice to reconnect with that side of myself.”

articles.title: Chat to strangers and let your kids be bored: how to embrace a ‘slow September’ – and enjoy life more
articles.summary: The pressure to self-optimise at the start of the new school year can lead to disappointment and burnout. Instead, here are seven ways to slow things down and reap the benefits. It is a hangover from our school days that September can feel like a time for getting back to the grind.
body: One antidote to this drive is to embrace a slower way of living. Rather than always rushing from one activity to the next, we could be enjoying life.

“In the age of digitisation, from work to socialising, we are seeing everything intensify,” says Heejung Chung, a professor of work and employment at King’s College London. “But by doing everything, we’re also creating a culture where it’s seen as normal. So you are not only creating a standard for yourself, but for everyone else as well. There is a creeping set of collective expectations that we can do everything, especially women, and we need to change it.”
So say “no” to self-optimisation this September, and instead embrace these practical ways to slow everything down – from work to parenting.

More often than not, we feel as though we don’t have enough time to converse with strangers in our daily lives, whether that be the woman next to you at the bus stop or the barista making your coffee. Yet taking the time to mindfully have a conversation with someone we don’t know has tangible benefits.

articles.title: Wide-legged trousers for men are having a moment. Just ask Gary Neville
articles.summary: Neville may have been mocked for wearing them on Monday Night Football, but he is actually bang on trend. From Kylian Mbappé’s World Cup style to Erling Haaland’s hair tie, football has had many viral fashion moments in 2026.
body: Perhaps the one that speaks to the fashion crowd, and a larger debate happening in menswear right now, is Gary Neville being mercilessly teased on Sky Sports’ Monday Night Football for sporting wide-legged trousers.

As a producer played Baggy Trousers, by Madness, Neville’s chino-style, wider-legged black slacks were mocked by fellow pundit Jamie Carragher, who compared Neville to Frank Worthington, the forward from West Yorkshire whose dandyish off-pitch style raised eyebrows in the 1970s.

“I went shopping in London,” Neville explained as Carragher jogged along to the Nutty Boys’ hit. “This guy styled me. I think they’re pretty cool, you know.” He predicted that Carragher would be wearing a pair soon.
Neville seems to be on to something. Because as far as the cut of your trousers goes, girth is greater.

articles.title: Steal My Food Itinerary: A Long Weekend in Upstate New York
articles.summary: I love New York City in the summer, especially this past one, but I grew up in the shadow of the Rocky Mountains. I’m in my late 20s, I rock climb, and I live in Brooklyn, so of course I have an upstate New York itinerary for you. My partner’s mom’s partner (yes) has a
body: Heading upstate this fall for autumn hikes and apple picking? Don’t sleep on all of the farm-to-table restaurants that the region has to offer.

When I tell people in the city about my trips upstate, they’re often surprised to hear me gush about the restaurants. And while I think you could make all your meals (the bounty at the farm stands and markets make cooking very dreamy up there) and still have a great time, I can also strongly make the case for a dining-focused trip. Here’s where to go.

If you’re heading up from the city, there are a few transit options (a bus from Port Authority to New Paltz or Kingston, the Metro North to Poughkeepsie, Amtrak to Hudson), but you’ll want a car to get around once you’re in the Catskills. I journey upstate via a car, which we pick up in New Jersey; that means that I get to grab Corner Slice’s massive, pillowy garlic knots as a pre-trip snack. If you find yourself in the area, I recommend you do the same.

articles.title: Unzipped: The Oral History
articles.summary: As this beloved documentary heads back to cinemas, Isaac Mizrahi, Douglas Keeve, and Nina Santisi—the film’s star, director, and producer, respectively, tell Vogue how it all came together back in 1995.
body: “Good news is good news and bad news is good news when you make a documentary,” observes Douglas Keeve, who directed Unzipped, the iconic fashion film that has been restored to be rereleased in theaters 31 years after its 1995 release. “It’s just about discovery, you know. You have to be a journalist, but you have to be innocent too. And try not to steer it, just try to capture it.”
Life might sometimes be stranger than fiction, but all storytellers—be they fantasists or documentarians—need some kind of action to propel their narratives forward.

The grain of sand around which Keeve forms his rare pearl of a movie is the negative fashion review designer Isaac Mizrahi, the film’s extrovert subject, received for his spring 1994 ready-to-wear collection. What follows is an examination of the largely associative and intuitive process by which the designer is driven to create a fall lineup that will bring the critics back around to his side.

articles.title: The Most Beautiful National Parks in Canada, From the Tourist Favorites to the Hidden Gems
articles.summary: Whether you want to paddle across a glacier lake, hike a mountain trail, or spot moose and bison, Canada’s national parks offer stunning settings for numerous outdoor experiences.
body: From the peaks of the Canadian Rockies to the deep woods of northern Ontario to the prairies where bison still roam, Canada ’s national parks span some seriously beautiful and ecologically important terrain. Since I moved to the Great White North more than 20 years ago, I’ve wanted to visit all of the country’s protected areas—and I’m now about halfway through the country's 37 national parks and 11 national park reserves.

Some of Canada's most stunning parks are well-known, like Banff National Park, where turquoise lakes, natural hot springs, and miles of mountain hiking trails draw more than four million visitors each year. Others, like Auyuittuq National Park in Nunavut’s Arctic wilderness, or Mingan Archipelago National Park Reserve in northeastern Quebec, are harder to reach and less trodden—but just as gobsmacking. Below, I’ve spotlighted 11 of the most beautiful national parks in Canada, from coast to coast, to inspire your own travel wish list. See what speaks to you, and I'll see you on the trails!

articles.title: Brave New Visions: Creativity as Rebellion. A Global Open Call by PhotoVogue
articles.summary: The PhotoVogue Global Open Call 2026 invites artists from all over the world to submit works that are an act of courage resisting against indifference.
body: We welcome photography, video, and multimedia projects across all genres, including fashion, documentary, portraiture, fine art, and experimental practices. We are looking for work that expresses a clear point of view, whether through the ideas it explores, the emotions it evokes, or the strength of its visual language. This can take many forms, from powerful storytelling to images that stand out for their aesthetic impact.
At a time when images are constantly produced and quickly forgotten, this open call invites artists to create work that resists repetition, holds attention, and makes something felt.
We are living through a time marked by violence, injustice, and acceleration. Wars continue. Atrocities unfold. Divisions deepen. Uncertainty grows.

And yet, even as the world becomes harder to bear, images move faster than ever. They accumulate, repeat, and dissolve. The more we see, the less we feel. A sense of déjà vu takes hold. A growing numbness. A quiet apathy.

articles.title: The DVF Awards Celebrated Extraordinary Women—and Honored the Legacy of Gloria Steinem
articles.summary: On Thursday evening, Venice's Teatro Goldoni provided the setting for a gathering of women who tend to make things happen rather than wait for them to happen: the 17th edition of the DVF Awards.
body: The chance to honor her legacy made for a poignant coincidence for an evening devoted to female power, and a reminder that, however much has changed since Steinem first began shaking things up, there is still plenty to do. Steinem’s spirit and presence were felt in a room designed, in many ways, in her image. “Gloria was gorgeous”, recalled von Furstenberg. “She was glory, her name was literally Glory. She was a glory, and she gave glory to women. She definitely earned her name. She stayed forever young, eternally a student. And such a badass. She refused to be a victim.”

It’s a lineage von Furstenberg herself has carried forward since 2010, utilizing her own awards platform to spotlight women who don’t simply talk about change—but get on with enacting it. Together with the Diller-von Furstenberg Family Foundation, the prize recognizes and support extraordinary women dedicated to transforming and inspiring the lives of other women, with each recipient granted $100,000 towards their nonprofit organization in order to further their work.

articles.title: How to Behave Yourself at the US Open
articles.summary: Like it or not, there are a few stringent matters of etiquette unique to the game that, as Naomi Osaka noted this week, need to be respected. So, herewith, our non-negotiable, no-nonsense rules for behavior at the US Open.
body: If that last part seems like a bit of an afterthought, we’ve got some helpful advice for you.

And, yeah, there have been issues. After a boisterous group armed with ring lights on stands seemed to be capturing content on the balcony of their suite during Naomi Osaka’s late-night opening match against Anastasia Zakharova—not between games or even between points, but while the players were competing —the baritone-voiced chair umpire, Kader Nouni (who is, incidentally, known among insiders as the Barry White of tennis), was forced to reprimand the group.
“Guys, please, in the suite behind me,” Nouni pleaded, his voice utterly bereft of sensuality or seduction, “please, thank you guys, please take your seat.”
